label: Frisk Extended to a Passenger Without Individualized Suspicion

trigger.description: Ask whenever the defendant was a passenger, to determine whether a frisk of that passenger was supported by suspicion specific to them, rather than general concerns tied to the stop itself.

all.question: q_frisk_suspicion_basis
value: General nervousness or presence in a high-crime area only
No suspicion articulated — officer cited only proximity to the driver or the stop itself

when.question: q_frisk_suspicion_basis
when.value: General nervousness or presence in a high-crime area only

review_conditions.display_note: Courts are split on whether generalized nervousness or a high-crime-area location, without more, can support a passenger frisk. This is a weaker record than 'no suspicion articulated' — confirm the full context of what the officer said before relying on this issue as written.

excluded_explanations.display_note: Passenger Frisk Without Suspicion was considered but not included: the passenger was ordered out of the vehicle but not frisked. Ordering a passenger out of a vehicle during a lawful traffic stop is permitted without any additional justification (Maryland v. Wilson, 519 U.S. 408 (1997)) — being ordered out, standing alone, is not grounds for suppression.

segments.text: A passenger frisk during a traffic stop requires more than the passenger's mere presence in the vehicle. An officer may frisk a passenger only where there is reasonable, articulable suspicion that the particular passenger is armed and dangerous, the standard set out in Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968). Arizona v. Johnson, 555 U.S. 323 (2009), confirms that this individualized standard governs passengers just as it governs drivers, and that general officer-safety concerns tied to the stop itself — without something specific to the passenger being frisked — do not satisfy it.

authorities.name: Terry v. Ohio
propositions: reasonable suspicion the person is armed and dangerous required for any protective frisk

authorities.name: Arizona v. Johnson
propositions: Terry frisk standard applies to passengers individually, not derivatively from the stop

segments.text: PLACEHOLDER — fill in once you've identified Alaska's controlling (or persuasive) authority on passenger frisks. Alaska may require an even more specific or contemporaneous basis than Johnson's federal floor.

practice_notes: Pin down exactly what the officer said or wrote to justify the frisk — vague references to 'officer safety' or the neighborhood, without anything tied to this specific passenger, are the weakest part of the government's position.
If the passenger was also asked for ID and that added time to the stop, that may raise a separate timing issue independent of the frisk itself.

A passenger has standing to challenge the stop itself and any search of their own person (Brendlin v. California, 551 U.S. 249 (2007)), but standing to challenge a search of the vehicle's contents is analyzed separately — don't assume one covers the other.
